prompt: Some governments now fund university places only in subjects that lead directly to employment. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
essay:
Public money for higher education is finite, and several governments have responded by directing it towards degrees with clear employment outcomes. I largely agree with this approach, although I would argue that judging a subject purely by the salaries of its graduates is too narrow a test of its worth.

The case for prioritising vocational and technical degrees is essentially practical. A country that trains too few nurses, engineers or software developers has to import that expertise at a premium, while graduates in oversupplied fields compete for the work they are overqualified for. Public funding is also a transfer from taxpayers, most of whom never attended university, and it is reasonable for them to expect a visible return in the form of services they actually use. Concentrating subsidy where shortages can be measured is therefore a defensible use of limited resources.

The difficulty is that employability is a poor predictor of long-term usefulness. Skills that look indispensable today can be automated within a decade, whereas the analytical and interpretive habits developed in history, philosophy or languages transfer across many roles. There is also a public interest that no salary figure captures: a society with no historians loses the ability to examine itself. These disciplines are also cheap to teach, so withdrawing support from them saves relatively little while risking a great deal.

My own view is that funding should follow demonstrated national shortages, but with a protected minimum for subjects that would otherwise disappear from the system altogether. Employment should guide public spending on universities without being allowed to dictate it entirely.
title: Funding only the degrees that lead to jobs
